name: Practical BFT
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Making the Generals Problem Fast Enough to Use
lesson.summary: Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance, introduced by Miguel Castro and Barbara Liskov in 1999, was the first algorithm to solve the Byzantine Generals Problem efficiently enough to run in real, working computer systems.
lesson.body:
For years after the Byzantine Generals Problem was formalized, known solutions were considered too slow and message heavy for practical use, which was a real obstacle since the problem was not going away, it was only becoming more relevant as distributed systems grew. In 1999, Miguel Castro and Barbara Liskov published Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance, usually shortened to PBFT, an algorithm specifically engineered to reach Byzantine fault tolerant agreement with performance closer to ordinary networked software than to a theoretical exercise. As the name promises, the goal was practicality: something engineers could actually deploy.

PBFT works with a fixed, known group of participants, called replicas, one of which acts as a leader for a given round and proposes the next value to agree on. Agreement moves through three message phases. In the pre prepare phase the leader broadcasts its proposal. In the prepare phase, replicas share that proposal with each other and confirm they all received the same one. In the commit phase, once a replica sees enough matching confirmations, it commits to the value and tells everyone else it has done so. Only once a replica collects enough matching commit messages does it treat the decision as final and irreversible.

That three phase structure directly answers the trap from the generals thought experiment, where a traitor could tell different peers different things and deny it later. Because replicas broadcast what they received to each other during the prepare phase, rather than only trusting the leader's word, a dishonest leader or a dishonest replica trying to sow contradictory instructions gets exposed: honest replicas can compare notes and notice the mismatch before committing to anything. PBFT keeps this guarantee as long as strictly fewer than one third of the replicas are faulty, the same threshold described in the Byzantine Fault Tolerance chapter, and it can typically finish a round in a small, bounded number of message exchanges rather than requiring the network to wait indefinitely for stragglers.

A useful comparison is a corporate board of thirteen members voting on an urgent decision by phone, where up to four members might be compromised and trying to get different factions of the board to believe different outcomes were agreed. Under a PBFT style procedure, board members do not just trust what the chairperson tells them, they check with each other during a prepare round before treating a decision as locked in, which lets the honest nine members detect and route around the compromised four.

PBFT's biggest practical limitation is that it needs the group of participants to be known in advance and communicating relatively quickly with each other, which is workable for a fixed set of validators but does not scale cleanly to an open network where anyone can join anonymously. This is exactly why PBFT and its descendants show up heavily in permissioned blockchain systems with a known validator set, while open networks like Bitcoin lean on proof of work instead, and it is also why PBFT style voting rounds tend to produce a different, stronger guarantee about when a transaction is truly settled, the topic of the next chapter on finality.
